neighbours.label: A concessive adverb that opens a sentence to grant a point (Of course, ... / Certainly, ...) after a preceding claim, vs 'course' as a noun and 'of course' tucked inside a clause
fire: The museum was crowded on Saturday. Of course, the new exhibit had just opened.
The plan sounds simple. Of course it will cost more than they say.
Our town has changed a lot. Certainly, the old bakery is gone now.
The film runs nearly three hours. Of course, some scenes drag a little.
The team lost the opening match. Of course nobody expected them to win.
Housing prices keep rising here. Certainly, the new railway made a difference.
She practised every evening. Of course, it paid off at the concert.
The hotel was very expensive. Of course the view from the room was amazing.
quiet: The museum was crowded on Saturday because the new exhibit had just opened.
The plan sounds simple, but it will of course cost more than they say.
Our town has changed a lot, and the old bakery is gone now.
The film runs nearly three hours over the course of the evening.
The team lost the opening match on a muddy course.
Housing prices keep rising here since the new railway opened.
She practised every evening during her piano course.
The hotel was very expensive, but the view from the room was amazing.

predictions: ' course' / ' Certainly' opening a sentence after a claim reach 0.4-0.8; noun 'course' and mid-clause 'of course' stay under 0.1.
notes: Card: top 32 peak on ' course' x22 in 'Of course' opening a sentence, plus ' Certainly', ' true'. Probe: 'Of course there are' 0.792, 'Certainly, it was not' 0.546; mid-clause ', of course,' 0.029, 'It is true that' 0.039, golf course 0.025, cooking course 0.028, same text without the adverb 0.034.
